title: Biggest Lottery Winners: What Happened After They Won
description: They matched every number. Then what? The true stories of America's biggest lottery winners — the decisions, the surprises, and the complicated aftermath.
content:
The Day Everything Changed

Picture a Tuesday morning in a hospital break room. Mavis Wanczyk, a 53-year-old medical center employee from Chicopee, Massachusetts, had worked at the same hospital for 32 years. She checked her ticket. Then she called her boss and quit on the spot. No notice, no transition plan — just a phone call and a goodbye. That moment, more than any dollar figure, tells you something true about what it feels like when everything shifts at once.

The biggest lottery winners in American history didn't just receive money. They received a problem they had never been trained to solve, arriving without instructions, usually within 24 hours of the draw. Some handled it with remarkable calm. Some did not. All of them had to become different people whether they wanted to or not.

Who Were These People Before the Win

A West Virginia Contractor on Christmas Morning

Jack Whittaker was already a millionaire when he won $314.9 million in Powerball on December 25, 2002 — the largest undivided jackpot in U.S. lottery history at that time. He ran a successful pipeline and excavation company in Putnam County, West Virginia. He was 55, he had a family, and by most accounts he was a man who had built something real with his hands. The win didn't create his wealth — it multiplied it beyond any framework he had for managing it.

An 84-Year-Old Woman in Florida

Gloria MacKenzie was quietly living in Zephyrhills, Florida, when she purchased a Powerball ticket that turned out to be worth $590.5 million in May 2013. She was 84 years old, making her the oldest solo jackpot winner on record. By most public accounts, she had spent her life in ordinary circumstances — which made the contrast with what followed all the more striking.

A 24-Year-Old in Wisconsin

Manuel Franco was 24 when he won a $768.4 million Powerball jackpot in March 2019. He was young enough that his entire adult life — career, relationships, identity — was still being formed when the money arrived. He later told reporters he had been screaming and jumping around his house for days after checking the numbers, barely sleeping, unsure what was real.

A California Man Who Rewrote the Record Books

Edwin Castro claimed the single largest lottery jackpot in U.S. history — a staggering $2.04 billion Powerball jackpot won on November 8, 2022, in California. The drawing had rolled over dozens of times, capturing national attention. Castro, a California resident, chose the lump sum option, which after taxes represented a dramatically smaller but still historic amount. His win remains the benchmark against which every subsequent jackpot is measured.

The Moment of the Claim — Decisions Made in Hours

Between finding out you've won and walking up to claim the prize, winners face a compressed series of decisions that most people spend a lifetime never having to make. Do you take the lump sum or the annuity? Do you go public or stay anonymous? Do you hire a lawyer before you even tell your family? These aren't abstract financial planning questions — they're choices made while still in shock, often within days of the draw.

Mavis Wanczyk went public almost immediately, appearing at a press conference where she was visibly emotional, saying she was going to "just take it one day at a time." The Mega Millions winner who took home $1.537 billion on October 23, 2018 — a single ticket sold in South Carolina — did the opposite entirely, claiming the prize anonymously through a trust and never stepping in front of a camera. Both approaches were legal. Both reflected something real about what the winner valued.

The Merle and Patricia Butler story offers a different model. The Illinois couple won a $218.6 million share of a Mega Millions jackpot in March 2012 and waited months before coming forward — reportedly consulting attorneys and financial advisors before making any public appearance. They walked into the press conference prepared. That pause, those months of quiet deliberation, may have been the most important financial decision they made.

For those weighing their own hypothetical options, a lottery tax calculator can illustrate how dramatically the lump sum versus annuity decision affects the actual take-home amount — a gap that runs into the hundreds of millions at jackpot sizes like these.

The Long Game — What the Money Actually Did

The years after a major win don't follow a predictable script. Some winners receded entirely from public life and appear, by what little can be observed, to have landed somewhere stable. Others became cautionary entries in journalism syllabuses. What's consistent across nearly all documented cases is that the money itself wasn't the whole story — it was an amplifier of whatever was already there.

  • Mavis Wanczyk said publicly that she planned to take care of her family and "go hide in a hole somewhere" — a statement that turned out to be more literal than metaphorical. She has maintained a very private existence since claiming her prize.
  • Manuel Franco, at 24, stated in a press conference that he wanted to invest wisely, travel, and help his family. At that age, the money arrived before he had accumulated the professional framework — career, retirement planning, long-term identity — that most people use to organize finances.
  • Jack Whittaker's story became the most publicly documented example of a win unraveling. His subsequent years included legal troubles, theft of large sums from his vehicle, and profound personal losses within his family. He had given generously — reportedly donating to churches and creating a charitable foundation — but the scrutiny, the requests, and the losses compounded in ways that were widely reported and are part of the documented public record of his life after December 2002.
  • Gloria MacKenzie, at 84, took the lump sum. At her age, the annuity structure offered little practical advantage. She donated to her local community, according to reports, and largely disappeared from the public eye — perhaps the quietest exit among the biggest lottery winners on this list.

Tax liability shapes everything at these dollar amounts. Federal withholding, state taxes, and the gap between the advertised jackpot and the lump sum cash value can reduce a billion-dollar headline to something closer to $400–$500 million in actual take-home. For context, resources like all state lottery guides can show how dramatically state tax treatment varies — from states that exempt lottery winnings entirely to those that add another 10% on top of federal withholding.

The Most Human Moment

"I just went into my boss and said, 'I won't be coming in tomorrow.'" — Mavis Wanczyk, at her August 2017 press conference, describing the first phone call she made after confirming her $758.7 million Powerball win.

That call — impulsive, honest, unburdened by any financial strategy — may be the purest thing recorded about any of these wins. Before the attorneys, before the press conferences, before the tax forms: she just wanted out. She had worked in the same hospital for 32 years. The first thing the money did was give her permission to leave.

Lessons Without the Lecture

It would be easy to frame these stories as a morality play — the humble winners who stayed grounded versus the ones who lost their footing. But that framing flattens what are actually complicated, documented human lives. What can be drawn from the public record is more practical than moral.

The winners who appeared to navigate the transition most smoothly shared a few observable traits: they delayed their public claim, they assembled professional advisors before appearing at press conferences, and they made decisions about privacy early. The Butlers waited months. The South Carolina Mega Millions winner never appeared at all. These weren't coincidences.

The winners who went public quickly and without preparation — however understandably, given the shock — found themselves fielding requests and attention before they had any framework for responding to them. That's not a character flaw. It's a structural problem: nothing in an ordinary life prepares a person for the day they become the answer to other people's financial problems.

What the stories of the biggest lottery winners reveal, more than anything, is that the money arrives in an instant and the consequences unfold over years. The numbers on a ticket take seconds to match. Learning to live with what comes next takes considerably longer.
